stoneConservation.title: Stones Conservation
description: Conservation efforts often go unnoticed as they focus on preserving historical authenticity without altering a monument's appearance.
This discretion means the public, interested in maintaining built heritage, is often unaware of the work and challenges involved.
The type of intervention depends on the gravity and the kind of degradation that the stone experienced.
The experts analyse the stone conditions and pick the right procedures

consolidation.title: Consolidation
description: When the only  surface is scaling, the degradation is not considered severe and usually minimum intervention are needed
Application of consolidant products to increase the strength of the stone and mortar patches to close the gaps are used

scalingFixing.title: Scaling fixing
description: When the surface appears healthy but there is scaling a few cm in depth, fixing intervention is needed to prevent the scale from detaching completely.
A special system of combination of pins and consolidants is used and interventions are invidibles at the end

mortar.title: Mortar replacement
description: When the first centimetres of the surface is degraded and not preservable, the damaged part is replaced with special mortars.
To improve adherence and resistance, a special grid is constructed to “reinforce” the mortar.

substitution.title: Stone replacement
description: When the stone is highly damaged and/or has a great artistic and historic value, it is substituted entirely.
If historical relevants the substituted pieces is preserved in the lapidarium.

title: Conservation Strategies
description: The Lausanne Cathedral, as we see it today, is the result of centuries of ongoing conservation efforts.

This section will explore the evolution of preservation practices and the fascinating journey of conserving this architectural heritage, from the more invasive, stylistic restorations of the past to today's philosophy of minimal intervention.

title: Rainwater Management Features
description: The management of rainwater at the Lausanne Cathedral has been a critical aspect of its conservation throughout the centuries, primarily due to the use of molasse stone, which is particularly susceptible to decomposition when exposed to rain.

This necessity was emphasised by Viollet-le-Duc in his 1872 restoration plan, where he stressed the importance of preserving the materials in an absolute manner and directing the water to the ground, using numerous conduits arranged with the greatest attention.

molassesAndItsWeathering.title: Molasse and its weathering
description: The cathedral of Lausanne was built with a local molasse sandstone, that is particularly sensitive to water.
You may obtain directly here information on that stone as well as on its weathering by clicking on the corresponding buttons
You may also go directly to an interactive discovery App to use as you walk around the cathedral.

molasseSandstone.title: The Molasse Sandstone
description: The Swiss Molasse rock formation stretches north of the Alps from the Lake Léman region in the west of Switzerland to the Constance Lake in the east.
It comprises a variety of calcite- bound sandstones, which can contain swelling clays.
As part of this formation, the “Molasse grise de Lausanne” was extracted right outside the medieval city center and employed to erect the Lausanne Cathedral.

Over the centuries, sandstones of the same typology were brought in from different local quarries distributed around the medieval centre and employed for modification and maintenance works at the Cathedral.

stonesOfTheCathedral.title: Stones of the Cathedral
description: The Lausanne Cathedral is built from a variety of stones originating from different quarries all around Switzerland and some parts of Germany.

During the 19th century, the regional molasse sandstone of exposed architectural elements of the Cathedral was replaced with limestones and “harder” sandstones from the wider region of the canton Vaud.
In the 20th century, due to the scarcity of regional quarries, the general substitution of local molasse sandstone for maintenance and restoration became common practice.
A variety of replacement sandstones from Fribourg, Bern, Zug, and Hannover (Oberkirchen, Germany) were utilized in its place.

molasseGris.title: Molasses Gris
description: It is a molassic sandstone from Lausanne and was placed in the Cathedral in the 12th Century CE (Gothic period).
It is a type of sedimentary stone which is predominant on the south tower of the Transept. This sandstone most likely came from the nearby quarries.
This stone is particularly sensitive to water due to the presence of swelling clays.

geologicalInformation.title: Geological Information
description: The geology of Switzerland covers the Central Alps, a segment of the Alpine chain located between the Western Alps of France and Italy and the Eastern Alps of Italy, Austria and Germany.
In this segment the Alpine chain is particularly narrow, yet it contains all the major tectonic units and exhibits landmark landscapes and landforms for which the Alps are known.

To the north, the Swiss Plateau ex-tends from Lake Geneva to Bern, Zürich, and Lake Constance tapering off from around 600 to 400 m a.s.l. This plateau corresponds to what is called the Molasse Basin.
Click on the map to learn more about the different Molasse, the quarries and their characteristics.

The Molasse facies result from the alteration and erosion of the Alps during the Alpine orogeny and are made up of sands of particle size variable (from fine to coarse), and of mineralogy also variable (quartz, feldspars, with more than r less micas) cemented with calcite.
The geological processes involved in the formation of the Molasse Basin date back to the Oligocene and Miocene eras.
Four main groups can be identified according to the sedimentation conditions involved (marine or freshwater condition).

weatheringOfMolasse.title: Weathering of Molasse
description: The process of degradation is a complex system that involves different factors.
The weathering mechanisms are the physical/chemical processes involved in the degradation.
The degradation type (or patterns) refers to how damage manifest in a larger scale.

degradationTypes.title: Degradation Types
description: The different weathering mechanisms do not always have an univocal correlation with the degradation pattern observed.
These are strongly related to the micro-climate the stone is subjected to and in consequence their position in the building.
The compresence in the same point of different degradation pattern can lead their identification difficult.
The major degradation patterns observed on the cathedral can be classified according these four classes.

blackCrust.title: Black Crust
description: Black crusts are classified as kind of crust developing generally on areas protected against direct rainfall or water runoff in urban environment.
Black crusts usually adhere firmly to the substrate. They are composed mainly of particles from the atmosphere, trapped into a gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) matrix.

scaling.title: Scaling
description: Detachment of stone as a scale or a stack of scales, not following any stone structure and detaching like fish scales or parallel to the stone surface. The thickness of a scale is generally of millimetric to centimetric scale.
It can be observed in areas exposed both to rain and sun. It represents the most challenging degradation pattern to evaluate, understand and restore.

description: Lorem Ipsum Sandy Sit Amet.

biodeterioration.title: Biodeterioration
description: In the areas more hit by the rain or where water percolates, he microorganisms such as fungi and musses find their natural humid environment to proliferate.
The resultant damage is not extremely dangerous for stone preservation but can create unpleasant aesthetic drawbacks.

title: Weathering
Mechanisms
description: Water is involved in all types of mechanisms of stone weathering.
You can get further information on each of them by clicking on the corresponding buttons.

trappedWater.title: Trapped Water
description: Freezing water in porous materials can cause damage by various mechanisms.
The first and most dramatic is called “water entrapment.” It refers to a situation similar to that of a glass bottle filled with water and placed in a cooler.
In other words, freezing occurs from all sides, the liquid is trapped, and the increase in molar volume from liquid water to ice causes the bottle to break.
Such situations are rare on monuments, with the possible exception of fine decorative elements previously saturated with water, as finials and fountains.
Watch the video to know more.

hydraulicPressure.title: Hydraulic Pressure
description: Another situation also related to the change in molar volume is called "hydraulic pressure".

It occurs when growing ice pushes the liquid water still present through the porous network. The flow resistance leads to a pressure that depends on the size of the pores and the distance over which the water is pushed.
For molasse, the pore size is large, which reduces this pressure.

However, if these same stones are saturated with water, then the equivalent length of the saturated pores can be very large, which can lead to high hydraulic pressures if the cooling rate is fast enough.
Watch the video to know more.

crystallizationPressure.title: Crystallization Pressure
description: Another situation in which frost can be damaging is the crystallization pressure. Under such conditions, low temperatures developed over long periods of time would be most damaging. Such situations are to be expected in colder climates than in Lausanne.
Watch the video to know more.

temperatureGradient.title: Temperature Gradient
description: Coarse porous materials, such as molasse, can be damaged during freezing if a temperature gradient is sustained.

Water can then move from an unfrozen region to feed the growth of ice trapped in the pores of a frozen region. This is analogous to frost heave but also can cause damage in sedimentary building stones and in geological settings.

Related situations can lead to forming ice lenses between a moist substrate (stone cores) and a surface subject to temperature variations (façade). The growth of such lenses can accelerate the detachment of pre-existing scales without the temperatures having to be very low.
Watch the video to know more.

acidRain.title: Acid Rain
description: Atmospheric pollution, particularly acid rains, has been a serious problem for the durability of Historic Buildings in the past.
Stones containing calcite were attacked due to the dissolutions of these minerals in contact with the acid solutions.
In the case of Molasse sandstone, the binder component (made of calcite) could have been affected, increasing the detachment of the grains in the stone’s microstructure.

microDust.title: Microparticles and Dust
description: Another problem related to the pollution of the air, to whom effect was decreased in the last 30 years, is the presence of microparticles of dust from the combustion processes that deposit on the stones and/or are englobed in the efflorescence that are formed due to the crystallization of salts on the surface of the buildings.
This led to the formation of the so called “black crusts”.

swellingClays.title: Swelling Clays
description: The stone used in Lausanne Cathedral during the Middle Ages is Molasse sandstone. Its microstructure consists of different siliceous materials bound together by a calcite-clay binder.

The presence of swelling clay determines the formation of stress in the material during wetting and drying due to rain. This stress, in the case of pre-existing cracks, can propagate them and cause scaling.

Swelling clays, like smectite, are a particular type of clay that can absorb water and expand. They are part of the family of Phyllosilicates (or "sheet silicates"), a group of minerals that have a unique layered structure.
Imagine them as tiny, flat sheets stacked on top of each other like a deck of cards.

In the case of swelling clays, due to some particular asset of the layers, in contact with water, they have the ability to pull the water molecules in between their sheets, causing the entire stack to puff up or swell.
The consequence is the swelling of the entire stone.

cornices.title: Cornices
description: These are single-sloped elements, either horizontal or sloped, located at the eaves.

copings.title: Copings
description: These are double-sloped elements, horizontal or sloped, found at the apex of flying buttresses, abutments, arches, or gables.

chamferedDripEdges.title: Chamfered Drip Edges
description: These are string courses (indicating the internal floors) found on elevations or in archivolts of bays.

slopedRetreats.title: Sloped Retreats
description: These are located at each setback of a buttress, abutment, or massif. These elements consistently show a high degree of dysfunction due to exposure and erosion.

rotatingDripEdges.title: Rotating Drip Edges
description: TThese are located on polylobed (trefoil or quatrefoil) openings, and the rose window.

slopedSupports.title: Sloped Supports
description: These are found at the sill levels of the arched windows in the bays.

dripGlazes.title: Drip Glazes
description: These are found on certain lean-to parts of the cathedral.

quarry1.title: Molasse Grise de Lausanne
body: This rock type varies in color from grey to blue, with some yellow variegation. It has a medium to coarse grain size and consists of quartz, potassium feldspars, plagioclases, calcite, and occasionally dolomite, pyrite, and goethite.
This is the main facies used on Lausanne Cathedral, including the south tower of the transept.

quarry2.title: Molasse of Ursy
body: This facies, to which the name of Ursy molasse is attributed according to the archives, is a facies with flat stratifications alternating levels with fine grain size and coarse levels. This grey-green facies has a purplish-pink patina.
This facies is found only in the basal part of the south-east buttress of the east façade.

quarry3.title: Molasse Grise de Lausanne
body: This facies of the Aquitanian age is deposited in the southern part of the Swiss plateau in the USM geological unit (Lower Freshwater Molasse). The depositional environment is continental, in a low-relief floodplain environment, associated with forests, swamps and mean-shaped rivers.
